stem: A brass wire of length 4.5 m with crosssectional area of \(3 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{2}\) and a copper wire of length 5.0 m with cross sectional area \(4 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{2}\) are stretched by the same load. The same elongation is produced in both the wires. Find the ratio of Young's modulus of brass and copper.
solution:
For brass,
\(L_{B} = 4.5\) m, \(A_{B} = 3 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{2}\)
\(l_{B} = l\), \(F_{B} = F\)
\(Y_{B} = \dfrac{F_{B}\,L_{B}}{A_{B}\,l_{B}}\)
\(\therefore Y_{B} = \dfrac{F \times 4.5}{3 \times 10^{-5} \times l}\)
For copper,
\(L_{C} = 5\) m, \(A_{C} = 4 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{2}\)
\(l_{C} = l\), \(F_{C} = F\)
\(Y_{C} = \dfrac{F_{C}\,L_{C}}{A_{C}\,l_{C}}\)
\(\therefore Y_{C} = \dfrac{F \times 5.0}{4 \times 10^{-5} \times l}\)
\(\dfrac{Y_{B}}{Y_{C}} = \dfrac{F \times 4.5}{3 \times 10^{-5} \times l} \times \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-5} \times l}{F \times 5}\)
\(= \dfrac{18 \times 10^{-5}}{15 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.2\)

stem: A wire of length 20 m and area of cross section \(1.25 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{2}\) is subjected to a load of 2.5 kg. (1 kgwt = 9.8 N). The elongation produced in wire is \(1 \times 10^{-4}\) m. Calculate Young's modulus of the material.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the "Given" block prints \(L = 10^{-4}\) m, reusing the symbol it has already assigned to the wire's 20 m length; the quantity meant is the elongation \(l\). The substitution below uses both correctly and reaches the printed \(3.92 \times 10^{10}\), so the result is unaffected.]

Given,
\(L = 20\) m
\(A = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{2}\)
\(F = mg = 2.5 \times 9.8\) N
\(L = 10^{-4}\) m
To find: \(Y\)
\(Y = \dfrac{FL}{Al} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 9.8 \times 20}{1.25 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(= 3.92 \times 10^{10}\) N m\(^{-2}\)
_note: TYPESETTING DEFECT, transcribed verbatim: the fourth 'Given' line prints \(L = 10^{-4}\) m, using the same symbol L that the second line already assigns to the 20 m length. It is the ELONGATION l that is \(10^{-4}\) m — the stem calls it that, and the substitution two lines below correctly uses 20 for L and \(10^{-4}\) for l. Not answer-affecting: \(2.5 \times 9.8 \times 20 / (1.25 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{-4}) = 3.92 \times 10^{10}\), which is what the book prints. Independently re-derived and correct.

stem: A metal cube of side 1 m is subjected to a force. The force acts normally on the whole surface of cube and its volume changes by \(1.5 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{3}\). The bulk modulus of metal is \(6.6 \times 10^{10}\) N/m\(^{2}\). Calculate the change in pressure.
solution:
Given,
volume of cube \(= V = l^{3} = (1)^{3} = 1\) m\(^{3}\)
Change in volume \(= dV = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\) m\(^{3}\)
Bulk modulus \(= K = 6.6 \times 10^{10}\) N/m\(^{2}\).
To find: Change in pressure \(dP\)
\(K = V\dfrac{dP}{dV}\)
\(dP = K\dfrac{dV}{V}\)
\(dP = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{10} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-5}}{1}\)
\(dP = 9.9 \times 10^{5}\) N/m\(^{2}\)

stem: Calculate the modulus of rigidity of a metal, if a metal cube of side 40 cm is subjected to a shearing force of 2000 N. The upper surface is displaced through 0.5 cm with respect to the bottom. Calculate the modulus of rigidity of the metal.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem asks for the modulus of rigidity twice, once at its opening and again at its close.]

Given,
Length of side of cube \(= l = 40\) cm \(= 0.40\) m
Shearing force \(= F = 2000\) N \(= 2 \times 10^{3}\) N
Displacement of top face \(= \Delta l = 0.5\) cm \(= 0.005\) m
Area \(= A = l^{2} = 0.16\) m\(^{2}\)
To find: modulus of rigidity, \(\eta\)
\(\eta = \dfrac{F}{A\theta}\)
\(\theta = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.40} = 0.0125\)
\(\eta = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}}{(0.16\,\text{m}^{2}) \cdot (0.0125)}\)
\(= 1.0 \times 10^{6}\) N/m\(^{2}\)
_note: The stem asks for the modulus of rigidity TWICE — it opens 'Calculate the modulus of rigidity of a metal' and closes 'Calculate the modulus of rigidity of the metal.' Printed exactly so; a redundancy, not an ambiguity. The derivation is internally consistent and independently re-derived: \(2000/(0.16 \times 0.0125) = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\).

stem: The coefficient of static friction between a block of mass 0.25 kg and a horizontal surface is 0.4. Find the horizontal force applied to it.
solution:
[Textbook note: the stem asks only to "find the horizontal force applied to it" without stating a condition; what the printed solution computes is the LIMITING force of static friction, that is the least force that will just start the block moving.]

Given,
\(\mu_{s} = 0.4\)
\(m = 0.25\) kg
To find: Force
\(F = \mu_{s} \cdot N = \mu_{s} \cdot (mg)\)
\(F = 0.4 \times 0.25 \times 9.8\)
\(F = 0.98\) N
_note: The stem is loosely worded — 'Find the horizontal force applied to it' names no condition, and any force below the limiting value is an equally valid answer. What the solution computes is the LIMITING force of static friction, i.e. the least horizontal force that will just set the block moving. Printed as transcribed; the arithmetic is correct (\(0.4 \times 0.25 \times 9.8 = 0.98\)) and uses \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).
